paragraphs: Environment and pace | Work primarily involves on-site physical activity: indoors in a controlled environment daily, 79%; standing continually or almost continually, 47%; exposure to disease or infections daily, 43%; repetitive motions more than half the time, 42%; substantial freedom to schedule tasks, 58%; substantial freedom to make decisions, 51%; and coordinating or leading others not important at all, 29%. Shifts and facility use schedules drive the pace.

Boundaries with neighboring roles | This page covers only the precise occupation O*NET-SOC 37-2011.00, Janitors and Cleaners. Neighboring occupations such as dishwashers, first-line supervisors of housekeeping and janitorial workers, maids and housekeeping cleaners, landscaping and groundskeeping workers, and carpet installers differ in their objects of work, authorized scope, and responsibilities. They cannot be interchanged based solely on titles, and proxy categories cannot replace organizational authorization, qualifications, or ultimate responsibility.

Dishwashing | Core outputs are cleaned and organized food service utensils and areas. This occupation focuses on whole-building cleaning and routine maintenance; work scope and safety requirements differ, and shared cleaning skills do not imply identical responsibilities.

First-line housekeeping and janitorial supervision | Core outputs are scheduling, quality inspection, and personnel management. This occupation focuses on personal work execution; management duties and assessment scope differ, so roles cannot be interchanged based only on titles.

Housekeeping cleaning | Core outputs are cleaned and organized guest rooms and linens. This occupation explicitly excludes maids and housekeeping cleaners; objects and standards differ and must be checked separately.

Landscaping and groundskeeping | Core outputs are care of outdoor green spaces, vegetation, and grounds. This occupation focuses on indoor cleaning and facility maintenance; environments and tools differ substantially and cannot be applied interchangeably.

Positive signals | You can follow procedures to sweep, polish, shampoo carpets, dust, and remove refuse; check chemical and equipment conditions and identify stains and safety hazards; and preserve reviewable anomaly and repair-need records and hand work over accurately.

Caution conditions | Risk signals include mixing chemicals based on experience, neglecting equipment and electrical safety, inadequate wet-floor and work-at-height protection, failing to report damaged facilities and safety hazards, and unauthorized repairs or pesticide use. If physical demands, shift work, and chemical exposure are difficult for you to tolerate, treat them as practical costs requiring serious consideration.

Trial action | Practice with an entirely  floor and stain scenario: complete a cleaning sequence, chemical and equipment safety checklist, and anomaly reporting and handover records. Test through observable deliverables rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

Conclusion | This page provides no validation evidence that personality tests predict performance in this occupation. Continue checking against real tasks, responsibility boundaries, and reviewable deliverables rather than drawing conclusions from a single label.

Conclusion | RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help formulate questions; they cannot replace work samples, learning ability, qualifications, and actual performance evidence for this occupation. No tool conclusion constitutes a hiring, authorization, or appointment decision.
